title: SIAG/OPT Views-and-News 19(2), December 2008: SIAM OP08 (issue editor)
contribution: His first issue as SIAG/OPT Views-and-News editor: two OP08 articles (image registration; split-body cutting planes for mixed-integer linear sets) chosen to show the diversity of the activity group, with an editor's column stating his aims.
problem_entry: Editorial agenda, not a research problem: broaden the newsletter's appeal and increase the number of issues per year (p. 16).
key_idea: Curate one application-driven and one theory article from the SIAM OP08 conference, highlighting the second's conjectures and open problems (p. 16).
positioning: Takes over from Luis Vicente (2003-2008) and credits his eight issues (p. 16).
writing: Short, warm editor's column; states aims, summarizes each article in one sentence, invites contributions (p. 16).
limits_future: Service contribution only; the chair's thanks to 'Kurt and Sven' for OP08 (p. 15) suggests Leyffer co-organized the meeting, an inference.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Picks OP08 articles to highlight the group's diversity and points readers to conjectures and open problems; asks for special-issue suggestions.

transferable: When editing an issue or session, pair an application-driven article with a theory article and name the open problems in the editor's note (p. 16).
coauthors: none (issue editor); articles by Fischer, Haber, Modersitzki and by Andersen, Weismantel; chair's column by Ferris

quotes.text: My aim is to broaden the appeal of Views-and-News, and, with your help, increase the number of issues per year.
Both articles describe work presented at the SIAM Optimization Conference in Boston.

title: Branch-and-refine for mixed-integer nonconvex global optimization
contribution: A global method for nonconvex MINLP (motivated by optimal power flow) that replaces SOS approximations by piecewise polyhedral envelopes built on a unary/binary decomposition and refines them by branching on the original variables, with a finite epsilon-global convergence proof and tightness comparisons against McCormick and trigonometric underestimators.
problem_entry: OPF needs trig functions that BARON cannot handle (p. 4); SOS approximation wrongly declared the OPF MILP infeasible, shown by a 1-D sin/quadratic example (pp. 6-7), and needs p^n variables (p. 6).
key_idea: Decompose functions on the computational graph (k1 p + k2 p^2 SOS variables), shift each piecewise-linear piece by its analytic max error to get a valid envelope, and branch-and-refine on original variables with a fixed number of breakpoints (pp. 6-19).
assumptions: C2 possibly nonconvex g_i, finite bounds on all variables, equality constraints (inequalities said to be easy), trig domain in [0, 2pi]; Theorem 4.1 needs bounded discrete and nonlinearly-appearing variables (pp. 4, 9, 20).
proof_devices: Convergence by valid LP lower / NLP upper bounds plus finite integer branching and envelope error going below epsilon by differentiability (Theorem 4.1, p. 20)
Set equivalence of SOS bilinear envelope with McCormick and convex hull (Theorem 3.5, p. 14; Appendix p. 23)
Four-corner convex combination makes SOS exact for xy (Theorem 3.4, pp. 12-13)
Tiny NLP where shared SOS set is tighter than McCormick (-0.75 exact vs -3) (p. 14)
Area ratios vs Caratzoulas-Floudas underestimators 0.451 and 0.313 (Prop. 3.6, p. 15)
Closed-form envelope-area ratio refinement vs SOS branching > 1, midpoint optimal (Prop. 4.2, pp. 20-21)
experiments: none in this paper; 'early experiments' favour branching on problem variables and a careful study is deferred to a companion paper (p. 16).
positioning: Extends Beale-Tomlin and Martin et al. SOS approximation; contrasts with BARON and alphaBB, which cannot handle the trig functions (pp. 4-5).
writing: Problem-first: an application failure and a small counterexample motivate each design change; proofs of several propositions delegated to Wanufelle's thesis (pp. 6, 9, 11, 22).
limits_future: No numerical results; error formulas only for x^2, sin, cos, xy with generalization asserted (p. 11); decomposition loses accuracy (x1x2x3 example, p. 8); open: breakpoint and branch placement, cuts, adding McCormick (p. 23).

method_links.note: Smallest example (sin(x)=0 with a quadratic, one variable) shows exactly how SOS approximation fails; own decomposition's accuracy loss also shown with a 3-variable example.
Removes a restriction of the packaged global solver (BARON has no trig support), but by building a new relaxation framework rather than iteration-level integration.
Carries B&B/linearization competence into nonconvex global optimization; the carried toolkit is B&B and SOS modelling rather than filter-NLP methods.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: compare relaxations by measured gap (area/volume) and closed-form ratios
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Area ratios vs trigonometric underestimators; envelope-area ratio of refinement vs SOS branching; volume factor 3 for diagonal SOS branching.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: branch on original variables and refine the approximation at fixed size
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Branch-and-refine resets breakpoints after each branch on x or y instead of branching on SOS variables.

transferable: Shift each piece of a piecewise-linear approximation by its analytically computed max interpolation error so the MILP becomes a valid relaxation and cannot be wrongly infeasible (eq. 3.1, pp. 10-12).
Factor nonlinear functions on their expression graph into unary/binary pieces before building SOS/envelope relaxations (p^n -> k1 p + k2 p^2), and report the accuracy cost (p. 8).
Prove a new relaxation is no weaker than the standard one by set equivalence, then exhibit a tiny NLP where it is strictly tighter (pp. 14, 23).

quotes.text: In a preliminary implementation, the resulting MILP was wrongly declared infeasible, even though the nonlinear problem was feasible.
The key to its convergence is the fact that the envelopes are refined as we move down the tree.

title: Global and finite termination of a two-phase augmented Lagrangian filter method for general quadratic programs
contribution: QPFIL: a two-phase QP method (gradient projection on a bound-constrained augmented Lagrangian to predict the active set, then an equality-constrained QP step) whose inexactness and acceptance are controlled by a filter, with global convergence and finite active-set identification proofs and CUTEr experiments.
problem_entry: A QP solver for use inside large-scale SQP: active-set methods change one index per iteration, interior methods give ill-conditioned KKT systems for iterative solvers (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Use the augmented Lagrangian only to reach a bound-constrained problem for cheap gradient projection; enforce global convergence by a filter on (dual infeasibility, primal infeasibility) that replaces BCL forcing sequences; estimate the penalty from lambda_min(H) and sigma_min(A) (pp. 4-9).
assumptions: Possibly indefinite QP with a KKT point; compact iterates (Assumption 3.1); full rank A*; single limit point (Thm 3.7) or SOSC (Thm 3.8); strict complementarity and Cauchy decrease for finite identification (Thm 4.2); exact EQP solves for finite termination (Cor. 4.3) (pp. 3, 12-19).
proof_devices: Global convergence analysed on a first-order version that skips second-order steps (pp. 12, 14)
Filter lemma borrowed from Chin-Fletcher with f = eta, h = omega (Lemma 3.6, p. 14)
Finitely many active sets imply finitely many penalty updates (Lemma 3.5, p. 14)
Least-squares multiplier bounds by the dual residual (Lemmas 3.2-3.3, pp. 12-13)
Sharp penalty threshold and computable bound max{0,-lambda_min(H)}/sigma_min(A)^2 (Lemmas 2.2-2.3, pp. 7-8)
Breakpoint ordering on the projected-gradient path separates active (<= eps/tau) and inactive (>= tau/eps) indices (Thm 4.2, pp. 17-19)
experiments: CUTEr QPs up to 20,000 variables via TAO/TRON with a user-defined filter termination and PETSc GMRES; vs KNITRO and LOQO by major iterations and CPU; fewer iterations, more CPU, ~90% of time in the KKT solver (pp. 19-20).
positioning: A second-order version of LANCELOT-type BCL methods; related to SLP-EQP methods (Fletcher-Sainz de la Maza, Chin-Fletcher, Byrd et al.) and gradient-projection active-set prediction (More-Toraldo) (pp. 3-4).
writing: Anticipates the reader's objection ('the careful reader may ask why QPFIL uses both a filter and a penalty function') and answers it in one paragraph; states dissatisfaction with its own penalty estimate (pp. 4, 9).
limits_future: CPU time disappointing, traced to GMRES on KKT systems; sigma_min estimate expensive; open: gradient projection until filter-acceptable, value of second-order step far from solution, inexact KKT solves (pp. 9, 20-21).

method_links.note: Filter globalization carried into bound-constrained Lagrangian methods; global convergence enforced by the filter, not the augmented Lagrangian.
Chooses major iterations as the comparable unit and says why, reports the CPU loss, and finds its cause by profiling.
Filter test inserted into TAO through its user-defined termination interface; algorithm framed as two swappable kernels (TAO, PETSc).

transferable: Prove global convergence on the plain first-order version and let the filter decide whether the fast second-order step is accepted (pp. 12, 14).
Replace hand-tuned forcing sequences in augmented-Lagrangian methods by a filter on (dual infeasibility, primal infeasibility) (pp. 4-5).
With linear constraints, compute a penalty threshold from lambda_min(H) and sigma_min(A) instead of increasing rho blindly (pp. 7-8).
When comparing a research code with production codes, pick the unit in which they do comparable work, report the other unit too, and profile to explain the loss (pp. 19-20).
coauthors: Michael P. Friedlander (UBC); initial implementation by summer student Anatoly Eydelzon (acknowledged)

quotes.text: At this stage we are not interested in a direct comparison between QPFIL and these production-quality interior implementations; rather, we are interested in the number of iterations it takes for QPFIL to identify the optimal active set—KNITRO and LOQO serve as relative benchmarks.
In particular, the referees’ comments led us to Theorem 3.8 as well as refinements of Algorithm 2.

title: SIAG/OPT Views-and-News 20(1), December 2009: 'The Public Side Of Optimization' (issue editor)
contribution: His second issue as editor, themed on optimization in public life (school starting times and bus schedules; Facebook friend wheels as QAP), with an editor's column asking for short papers summarizing journal submissions.
problem_entry: Editorial theme: social-life problems modelled as optimization (unsigned introduction, p. 1).
key_idea: Curate two applied articles; solicit short summaries of SIOPT/Mathematical Programming submissions and hot-topic suggestions (p. 15).
writing: Brief, personal editor's column (holiday tradition, moved further West), then a direct call for contributions (p. 15).
limits_future: Service only; the OP11 call lists MINLP among its themes (p. 13, other people's text).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theme issue on the public side of optimization; asks for short summaries of journal submissions and new hot topics.

transferable: Fill a newsletter or workshop by asking authors for short versions of papers already submitted to journals (p. 15).
coauthors: none (issue editor); articles by Fugenschuh and by Bredendick, Ferris; chair's column by Ferris

quotes.text: Please consider submitting a short paper (maybe summarizing a paper that you submit to SIOPT or Mathematical Programming), or suggest new hot topics for the next issue.
I am fortunate to have received two interesting and well-written papers for this issue, but as always we need more papers.

title: Applications and algorithms for mixed integer nonlinear programming
contribution: SciDAC overview of MINLP applications (LHC thermal insulation, nuclear core reload), algorithm classes and software, arguing with two examples (perspective reformulation, multilinear convex hull) that strong reformulations decide tractability.
problem_entry: Current software often cannot solve practically sized MINLPs; aim to correct the mismatch between natural models and robust solvers (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Relax-and-search view of MINLP algorithms; strong reformulations: perspective hull for indicator sets (SQUFL 16,697 s/45,901 nodes -> 23 s/44 nodes) and multilinear convex hull (bound 36.33 vs 2.33 McCormick; feasible IPOPT start) (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: f, g continuously differentiable; X, Y compact polyhedral (p. 2).
experiments: Two illustrations: SQUFL timings assembled from two papers ([10], [8]) and one multilinear example solved with IPOPT and confirmed by BARON (pp. 5-6).
positioning: Survey-level; credits Gunluk-Linderoth for the perspective hull and Sherali for multilinear hulls; contrasts with the 'textbook' McCormick route (pp. 5-6).
writing: Application pictures first, then algorithm taxonomy and software table, then two short reformulation stories; hedged 'This example suggests' (pp. 3-6).
limits_future: No explicit limitations or future work; evidence is illustrative (one example; cross-paper timing comparison) (pp. 5-6).

method_links.note: Formulation decides solvability: over 700x speed-up from the perspective reformulation; the hull relaxation gives both a better bound and a good NLP start.
Evidence for the hull approach is a single example hedged as 'suggests'; the SQUFL speed-up combines numbers from two separate papers.

transferable: Show a reformulation matters by reporting the same instance and solver before and after, in time and nodes (p. 5).
Judge a relaxation by its bound and by whether its solution is a good starting point for a local NLP solver (p. 6).
coauthors: Jeff Linderoth (corresponding), James Luedtke, Andrew Miller, Todd Munson

quotes.text: Our research is aimed at correcting the mismatch between natural optimization models and available robust optimization solvers.
The speedup factor is more than 700.

title: Optimization of 3D plasmonic crystal structures for refractive index sensing
contribution: FDTD study of how geometry and gold thicknesses of a 3D plasmonic crystal affect refractive-index sensitivity, ending with a trust-region quadratic-surrogate derivative-free search that raises the predicted figure of merit to 18,700 nm/RIU, about ten times the earlier design.
problem_entry: Many interacting geometric parameters, no simple physical prediction, and FDTD runs of up to 6 h on 128 processors (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: One-parameter sweeps first, then a Powell-style least-change-Hessian quadratic surrogate in a trust region, seeded with the sweep data and refined at each predicted optimum (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: FOM = slope of integrated normalized transmission change vs refractive index (eq. 1); 4 nm FDTD grid; derivatives unavailable from FDTD (pp. 2, 4, 5).
experiments: Simulated trends checked against fabricated samples where possible (experimental FOM up to 2x smaller); DFO: 8 iterations to +13%, 10 more without gain; control structures isolate contributions (pp. 4-6).
positioning: Builds on the group's earlier plasmonic crystals (refs 1, 11) and cites Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente and Powell for DFO (pp. 1, 5).
writing: Chemistry-journal style: methods, systematic parameter sections, then optimized structures; claims of optimality phrased as beliefs (p. 6).
limits_future: Optimal gold geometry hard to fabricate; only qualitative agreement with experiment; local optimum not certified (81 runs prohibitive); future: well shape, longer wavelengths, extend DFO (pp. 5-7).

method_links.note: Home NLP/DFO toolkit (trust-region quadratic models after Powell) carried into an expensive physics simulation.
Calibrated stopping claim stated as a belief, with the reason and the cost of a proper local-optimality certificate.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: seed the surrogate with the sweep data
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Coordinate-wise parameter sweeps are reused as the initial interpolation set of a trust-region quadratic surrogate.

transferable: For an hours-per-run simulator, do cheap one-parameter sweeps first, then fit a trust-region quadratic surrogate to those points and simulate only at its predicted optima (pp. 5-6).
When optimality cannot be certified, state what certification would cost and phrase the claim as a belief (p. 6).
coauthors: Joana Maria, Tu T. Truong, Jimin Yao, Tae-Woo Lee, Ralph G. Nuzzo, Stephen K. Gray (corresponding), John A. Rogers (corresponding); Leyffer's role inferred to be the DFO step

quotes.text: However, we cannot apply gradient-based optimization methods, because the FDTD simulations preclude the accurate and efficient computation of derivatives.
We interpret the fact that our local surrogate does not improve the FOM over 10 consecutive iterations as an indication that the design cannot be improved locally.

title: Mixed-integer support vector machine
contribution: An L0-norm feature-selecting SVM formulated with indicator variables and perspective constraints; after diagnosing a Slater CQ failure that makes MINLP solvers fail, it is relaxed to a big-M MIQP and compared with five SVM feature-selection methods on four UCI sets.
problem_entry: L1-SVM selects features only as a by-product and biases weights; L0-SVM is NP-hard and earlier work only approximates it (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Indicators z_j with perspective constraints w_j^2 <= z_j u_j (MIQCQP); when direct MINLP solves fail, read the failure as a CQ violation at z_j = 0 and reformulate to |w_j| <= M z_j (MIQP), then refit an SVM on the selected features (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Linear binary SVM; at least one feature selected; fixed M = 10^4; as printed, (P1) keeps 1/2 e^T u in its objective without the constraint defining u (pp. 3-4).
experiments: Ionosphere, WPBC24, WPBC60, SPECTF; 10-fold CV; baselines SVM, RFE, L1-SVM, FSV, R2W2 (three self-coded in MATLAB); CPLEX 11.1; MI-SVM2 best average accuracy 77.7% with 20.8 features, but below plain SVM on WPBC60 (pp. 4-5).
positioning: Embedded feature selection; builds on Gunluk-Linderoth perspective relaxation; cites 'In defense of l0' for the right-problem argument (pp. 1-3).
writing: Workshop-paper brevity; the solver-failure diagnosis is given in plain words with the CQ named (p. 3).
limits_future: Is big-M the best approximation of the conic constraints; scalability limited by CPLEX (p. 5).

method_links.note: Solver failures read as a Slater CQ failure at z_j = 0; formulation repaired (big-M) before any algorithm change; notes that preprocessing w_j^2 <= 0 to w_j = 0 would also fix it.
Sparse SVM recast into a home class (MIQCQP/MIQP with indicators and perspective constraints).
Self-built baselines and a written tuning rule, but the 'generally more predictive' conclusion rests on averages over four sets, one of which (WPBC60) goes against it.

transferable: When a MINLP solver fails on an indicator/perspective model, check whether z = 0 turns a convex constraint into one with empty interior (w^2 <= 0, Slater fails) and preprocess it to an equality or big-M form (p. 3).
After a mixed-integer selection step, refit the continuous model on the selected support rather than thresholding the mixed-integer solution (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: We believe that the failure of the nonlinear solvers is due to a failure of a constraint qualification
The errors that we observe from the nonlinear solvers are consistent with a failure of a constraint qualification.

title: A complementarity constraint formulation of convex multiobjective optimization problems
contribution: Finding a maximally uniform discrete representation of a convex Pareto set is written as a bilevel problem and, via first-order conditions of SUM(w) or GOAL(z), as an MPCC solved as an NLP with filterSQP, with an MPCC-LICQ result, a published test set and generator, and a failure-coded computational study.
problem_entry: Uniform weights do not give a uniform Pareto set (Das-Dennis); choose weights or goals optimally (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Upper level maximizes Sayin's uniformity over q Pareto points; lower level q single-objective NLPs replaced by KKT conditions under convexity; MPCC solved as NLP with slacks; feasible start from PATH on the fixed-weight NCP (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: A1 C2; A2 nonempty bounded feasible set; A3 MFCQ and SOSC at single-objective solutions; A4 convexity, 'the most restrictive' (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: Pareto optimality of MPCC solutions as a corollary of Miettinen-Makela conditions (Cor. 2.1, Prop. 2.2, p. 5)
LICQ + SOSC of the single-objective NLP imply linearly independent active normals of its KKT complementarity system, by contradiction on the basis matrix (Prop. 2.3, pp. 5-6)
One-variable two-objective nonconvex counterexample where the MPCC selects a maximizer (eq. 13, p. 6)
experiments: 11 literature problems plus 3 random convex MOQPs from his generator (all online); q = 10; PATH + filterSQP; failures coded [S]/[I]/[L]; goal formulation best; BARON on ex005 (q = 8) brackets 0.3032-0.7055 in 36,000 s while MPCC finds 0.3580 in 0.04 s (pp. 6-9).
positioning: Builds on Sayin's quality measures and on the MPCC-as-NLP results of Fletcher-Leyffer(-Ralph-Scholtes), Anitescu and others; acknowledges a referee for the weak-dominance point about SUM(w) (pp. 2-5).
writing: States assumptions, then rates them ('most restrictive'); reports failures and 'surprising' results plainly; lists open questions as concrete engineering obstacles (pp. 3, 8-9).
limits_future: Users must derive KKT conditions by hand (error prone); spurious Pareto points without convexity; q^2 constraints limit to about 10 points; AMPL bilevel support would need third derivatives; future: decomposition of objective space, interactive NIMBUS use (pp. 9-10).

method_links.note: The MPCC-as-NLP base (filterSQP, strong stationarity of the slack NLP) carried into multiobjective optimization; the base is what makes the approach practical.
His own method gets a one-variable breaking example showing where convexity (A4) is needed; the failure mode gets its own code [L] in the results.
Test problems and the random MOOP generator published on his web page.
Failures kept in the results table with a per-instance code; a global solver used to bracket the optimum on the smallest instance.
Slack formulation chosen to be numerically favourable; warm start from an NCP because cold MPCC solves fail to find feasible points.

transferable: To choose parameters of a family of subproblems optimally, write a bilevel problem, replace the convex lower level by KKT conditions, and solve the MPCC as an NLP with slacks (pp. 3-5).
Warm-start a hard MPCC from an NCP solved with upper-level variables fixed, retrying until the start is non-degenerate (p. 6).
Run a global solver with a time cap on the smallest instance only to bracket the optimum, and report its bounds beside the local result (pp. 8-9).

quotes.text: Surprisingly, the local MPCC solver finds a better solution than the global optimization approach.
We have observed examples where a lack of convexity results in spurious Pareto points being found by our approach.
